title: The valley spirit
hookLine: the valley spirit never dies; it is the mysterious female (Tao Te Ching 6)

lines: THE LOW PLACE IS WHERE THINGS GROW.
cards: Hikers climb the peak for the view, take the photograph, and head back down. Nobody stays up there. The farms are below, in the valley: the river, the deep soil, the orchards, smoke from kitchen chimneys.
The high place is admired. The low place is where things grow. Chapter six of the Tao Te Ching is barely a few lines long, and it chooses the valley as its picture of something that never dies.

teach.b: First, the valley never dies. Legge put this chapter into rhyming verse, and it begins: "The valley spirit dies not, aye the same." A valley is a hollow, defined by what isn't there.
Because it's low and open, it keeps receiving rain, snowmelt and rivers, and it doesn't wear out.
Second, the mysterious female. The chapter names the valley spirit the mysterious female, the dark mother.
The book reaches for a picture of birth: the Tao not as a ruler giving orders from above, but as a mother from whom everything comes, low and hidden and endlessly giving. Third, its gate is the root.
The gate of this mysterious female, the chapter says, is the root of heaven and earth.
That's the third gate in a week: the border gate, the gate of the mystery in chapter one, and now this, each an opening, not a wall.

One old commentary, traditionally credited to a figure called Heshang Gong, reads the chapter in the body: the valley nourishing the spirit, and the gate as the nose and mouth, where breath comes and goes.
Other readers keep it as a picture of the world. Fourth, used gently.
This power goes on unbroken, the chapter ends, used gently, without strain.
The valley never forces anything. It stays low and open, and the water arrives.

how: Some Taoist practitioners connect chapter six with gentle breathing practice, following an old commentary that reads the gate of the mysterious female as the nose and mouth; other readers take it as a picture of the world's source.

games.q: you're water falling on a mountain. where do you end up?

games.why: the water runs down and gathers in the valley. chapter six chooses the valley, low and open, as its picture of what never dies.

practice: Get low if you can: sit on the floor, lie down, or lean back and let something take your weight. Breathe gently through the nose and notice the breath arriving on its own, the way water arrives in a valley without being called.
If you pray, you can pray from this low place; if not, simply rest there.

wordCard.voice: The valley spirit. Chapter six's picture of what never dies: low, open, receiving, the mysterious female whose gate is the root of heaven and earth. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, gǔ shén: the valley spirit, from Tao Te Ching 6, which says it never dies.
